cells.tense: You are moving with what you can see, one step at a time, and the step keeps teaching you.
cells.ask: Take the next small step in the direction you're already leaning — a call, a sketch, a sentence — before you're certain. Let the step itself show you what you were reaching for.
cells.core:
You can work without the whole picture. Not because you're reckless, but because you've learned that enough light for one step is enough, and the step itself teaches you what you were reaching for. The imagining and the walking have become one motion — you dream something, you move, and the move shows you what the dream was.

That's rarer than it sounds. Most people either wait for the full map or move and lose track of what they were reaching for. You're doing both at once, and the satisfaction runs on that. It isn't that everything worked out perfectly; it's that what you pictured has been felt in practice. Keep feeding it. The next step is usually closer than the shape of it suggests.
cells.sheetLine: You walk by the light you have, not the light you want.
cells.verb: imagining something until it feels fully real
cells.place: somewhere between not enough light to see and enough to take the next step

cells.tense: You are leaning into a future where this is finally done, bracing for a satisfaction you haven't reached yet.
cells.ask: Pick one piece of what you're imagining and stop improving it for a day. Let it be as finished as it is right now, and notice what it's already made of.
cells.core:
You're pushing toward what this could become, and the pushing has taken over. The version ahead feels nearly settled — you can almost taste the satisfaction on the other side of it — and that's exactly what keeps you from the one in front of you. Every idea gets another pass, another angle, another adjustment that might finally make it right.

What you're chasing is the feeling of having fully pictured and fully felt something. That feeling doesn't come from imagining harder. The hunger isn't for a better version. It's the refusal to let anything be complete while a slightly better one still lives in your head. Set one thing down as it is. That isn't giving up on it.
cells.sheetLine: You're improving the dream faster than you can feel it.

cells.tense: You were close to something that mattered, and you are still standing back from it.
cells.ask: Put one thing in front of someone this week — a rough sketch, a half-formed plan — and hear what they say instead of working it out alone.
cells.core:
The imagining has gone quiet somewhere. Not because there was nothing to imagine, but because the next step meant putting an unfinished thing where someone could see it, and that's the part that stalled. You can't tell which version is worth building, so none of them gets built, and the whole thing waits.

You don't need a clearer sign. You need one small piece of the work to leave your hands and land somewhere real. That's how direction comes back — not from resolving the whole picture, but from letting one rough thing be seen and hearing what it makes in someone else. What you want hasn't gone anywhere. It's just been waiting for the next move to be smaller than it looks.
cells.sheetLine: One unfinished thing, shown to someone, finds more than thinking does.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what is coming together, and you talk about it as if it were assembling itself.
cells.ask: Name one choice you made this week that actually went the way you wanted, and say out loud that you did that. Not the timing, not the luck. You.
cells.core:
The work is happening — imagining things into shape, feeling them through, letting satisfaction land where it's earned. But you'd probably describe it as just happening. The ideas arrived, the pieces fit, it worked out. You don't take the pen for any of it.

That's what makes this hard to see: when it's running well, the dreaming and the doing feel like one motion, clean enough that you can't tell where you ended and the flow began. But you did bring it together — your attention, your patience, your willingness to feel it through to the end. Calling that yours isn't arrogance. It's just accuracy.
cells.sheetLine: You did bring this together. Say so out loud.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person's visions and dreams have actually been realized well enough for satisfaction to be warranted — I only know the capacity is present, not what it has produced. A reader could reasonably say the imagining hasn't happened yet or that the contentment is theirs to define, not mine. The asks survive being wrong: each one is a step a person can take regardless of whether my read of their state is correct, and none makes relief conditional on obeying. The sentence that serves me more than them is the too-much cell's sense that the dreaming has become the relationship — it sounds incisive but it could read as a judgment on their process; I've kept it as description of a bend, not a verdict.
